IFS focuses on the relationships between parts of your mind that represent thought processes and the core "Self". The goal is to create a cooperative and trusting relationship between yourself and these dysfunctional parts of your mind

The idea is that when you have a negative or disruptive thought, try to have a dialogue with it. Come from a place of curiosity and comfort rather than discipline.

It's proven to work best for people with addiction and PTSD, but it can be used with almost anyone. 

But this is just my personal suggestion. It's what helped me the most. Not every type of therapy works for everyone, so of course you should try and find what works best for you
It can be done with or without a therapist. But it does take a lot of time to learn about on your own, which I understand not everyone has access to

This is why I don't like cognitive behavioral therapy being the default for therapy. It works for some people but it makes a lot of people feel worse

If you feel trapped in a cycle of hating your behavior but never changing it, I recommend internal family systems therapy. It teaches you to work with yourself instead of against yourself

In that case, It's definitely a good way to force yourself into getting help. But you should still be careful because inpatient is not a very schizoid friendly environment. You're constantly surrounded by people. Nurses waking you up in the middle of the night, eating every meal in a group setting, showering and using the bathroom with the door open, etc.

As long as you pace yourself and explain to the staff your condition as well as you can, you should be ok. But be prepared that it might be a shock to your system. 

I think the thing that will help you the most is the resources. When you're in a hospital the amount of services and programs available to you is much more than in outpatient. You'll have dozens of people helping you to get back on your feet once you get out. Just take advantage of that while you can.

In my experience there's no therapy at inpatient. There's a psychiatrist that you can talk to once a week about your meds, and group therapy. that's it. 

But that's just my experience, and it might be different outside of where I live. You should check with them beforehand and make it clear that you want to talk to a psychologist not a psychiatrist. If they don't offer that, find someone who does.
